input_signals.name: Externally Financed Tangible Expansion Without Knowledge
input_signals.hypothesis: Raising outside equity and debt to fund expansion is most value-destructive when the firm has no knowledge-based competitive advantage to deploy the capital against.
input_signals.reasoning: External financing predicts low returns partly because managers issue when overvalued, but R&D-rich firms have genuine funding needs for intangible projects that markets ration. The multiplicative rank interaction fires only when heavy external financing coincides with low R&D-to-sales, distinguishing opportunistic capital raising from knowledge-driven financing.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( add( sstk, delta( dltt, 1 ) ), at ) ), rank( neg( ratio( coalesce( xrd, 0 ), sale ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Capex Acceleration Minus R&D Acceleration
input_signals.hypothesis: A firm accelerating physical capital spending while simultaneously decelerating knowledge investment is late in its investment cycle and reallocating toward commoditized capacity, foreshadowing declining profitability and low returns.
input_signals.reasoning: Second-difference framing captures the reallocation decision at the margin rather than the level of investment intensity, which is heavily industry-determined. Managers cut discretionary R&D first when they chase near-term capacity, so the wedge between the two accelerations is an early-warning composition signal not visible in either investment or intangible level.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: sub( accel( ratio( capx, at ) ), accel( ratio( coalesce( xrd, 0 ), at ) ) )

input_signals.name: Physical Expansion During Own-History R&D Retrenchment
input_signals.hypothesis: Gross plant expansion is most value-destructive when the firm has simultaneously pushed its own R&D intensity to a five-year low, indicating capital is being redirected from innovation into commoditized capacity.
input_signals.reasoning: This repairs the earlier validator failure by anchoring the investment leg on gross PP&E (an investment-exclusive variable) rather than total assets, while the intangible leg is a within-firm time-series position, so a chronically high-R&D firm at its own knowledge trough is flagged as strongly as a perennial non-innovator. Both legs are non-negative cross-sectional ranks, so the product is monotone and cannot flip sign, and the short leg concentrates on firms scaling hard capacity precisely as they disinvest in knowledge.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( growth( ppegt, 1 ) ), rank( neg( ts_rank( ratio( coalesce( xrd, 0 ), sale ), 5 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Plant Growth Deflated by Knowledge-Inclusive Capital
input_signals.hypothesis: The overinvestment penalty attaches to physical capital accumulation measured against the firm's true (tangible plus unbooked knowledge) capital base, so identical dollar plant additions are far more aggressive for firms with no R&D stock than for knowledge-rich firms.
input_signals.reasoning: The intangible theme enters through the deflator rather than a multiplicative weight, keeping the construct monotone with a strictly positive denominator and no sign-flip risk; this is the scaling-design repair of the earlier rejected idea, now grounded in ppent rather than assets. It isolates a clean question the archive has not answered: whether capitalizing R&D into the denominator sharpens the physical-investment penalty relative to conventional asset scaling.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: ratio( delta( ppent, 1 ), add( ppent, ts_sum( coalesce( xrd, 0 ), 5 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Capacity Expansion Without Pricing Power
input_signals.hypothesis: Heavy reinvestment in physical capacity is value-destructive precisely for firms lacking an intangible moat, proxied by a persistently thin gross margin, because added capacity in a commoditized product market cannot earn rents.
input_signals.reasoning: This abandons both the change-of-share framing that made the flagged proposal a near-restatement of the capex-minus-R&D acceleration signal and the unstable COALESCE(xad, 0) term whose appearing-and-disappearing reporting corrupted a differenced measure. It measures the intangible side through realized pricing power — a three-year average gross margin, which is the economic output of brand and know-how rather than its accounting input — so it tests whether the moat, not the R&D line item, is what conditions the investment penalty, and it applies to the full sample including firms that never report R&D.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( capx, ppent ) ), rank( neg( ma( ratio( sub( sale, cogs ), sale ), 3 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Asset-Light Knowledge Scaling
input_signals.hypothesis: Firms that expand revenue without expanding gross plant, and that have an accumulated R&D stock capable of explaining how, are monetizing unbooked knowledge capital whose scalability the market underprices.
input_signals.reasoning: Every archive signal so far is short-side and negative-signed, leaving the long side of the intangibles story untested; this construct is deliberately built on revenue growth rather than asset growth so that it is not simply the mirror image of the FF5 investment factor, which absorbed the plant-growth signals that had strong slopes but zero alpha. The interaction is essential: sales growth without plant growth is ambiguous alone, and R&D intensity alone is a documented level effect, but jointly they identify knowledge-driven operating leverage.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( sub( growth( sale, 1 ), growth( ppegt, 1 ) ) ), rank( ratio( ts_sum( coalesce( xrd, 0 ), 3 ), sale ) ) )

input_signals.name: Erratic Capex Without Knowledge Anchor
input_signals.hypothesis: Unstable physical investment reflects reactive, opportunity-chasing capital allocation, and it is most damaging in firms with no sustained knowledge program to give the spending strategic direction.
input_signals.reasoning: This introduces a second-moment investment channel absent from the archive, which has tested only levels, changes and accelerations, and the FF5 investment factor prices the level of investment rather than its instability, so the spread has a plausible route to surviving as alpha. The knowledge stock enters as the anchor that distinguishes lumpy but purposeful capacity building in innovative firms from erratic allocation in firms with no research program.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( vol( ratio( capx, ppent ), 5 ) ), rank( neg( ratio( ts_sum( coalesce( xrd, 0 ), 5 ), sale ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Plant Contraction With Research Intensification
input_signals.hypothesis: A firm simultaneously shrinking its physical capital base and raising research intensity is executing a deliberate pivot from replicable hard assets toward knowledge capital, and because the R&D is expensed while the plant reduction is visible, reported fundamentals understate the transition and returns are subsequently high.
input_signals.reasoning: The critic's two objections are both structural and both fixed: the horizons are now matched — a one-year plant change against a one-year change in research intensity — and the intangible leg is a within-firm change rather than a level, so the signal is orthogonal to the published R&D-intensity anomaly and cannot be a monotone transform of it. The interaction is essential because plant contraction alone is often distress and rising research intensity alone is often a sales collapse in the denominator, whereas their conjunction identifies genuine reallocation; both legs are non-negative cross-sectional ranks so the product is monotone in each channel.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( neg( growth( ppent, 1 ) ) ), rank( delta( ratio( coalesce( xrd, 0 ), sale ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Knowledge-Backed Gross Profit Scaling
input_signals.hypothesis: Firms that expand gross profit without expanding plant, and that hold a research stock capable of explaining the source of that expansion, are converting unbooked knowledge capital into rents the market has not capitalized.
input_signals.reasoning: Asset-Light Knowledge Scaling is the archive's only joint-strength long-side result (fmb 2.4, alpha 2.8%, t 2.5), and the critic's diagnosis was that its raw sales-growth leg fights the signal because unprofitable revenue growth is itself a negative predictor; replacing sales growth with gross-profit growth keeps the asset-light scaling concept while filtering out margin-dilutive expansion. This is a targeted quality refinement of a proven mechanism rather than a new template, and it should improve both the slope and the alpha if the original leg was contaminated as diagnosed.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( sub( growth( sub( sale, cogs ), 1 ), growth( ppegt, 1 ) ) ), rank( ratio( ts_sum( coalesce( xrd, 0 ), 3 ), sale ) ) )

input_signals.name: Gross Profit Per Employee Without Plant
input_signals.hypothesis: Rising gross profit per employee achieved without expanding physical plant is the fingerprint of organizational and human capital — intangible assets that never enter the balance sheet — and firms displaying it earn abnormal returns as the productivity gain proves durable.
input_signals.reasoning: The archive has proxied intangibles only through R&D spending, goodwill and gross margin, never through labor productivity, even though human and organizational capital is the largest unbooked intangible category for most firms; employment is broadly reported, so this avoids the zero-mass problem that flattens the R&D-gated signals. The interaction is necessary because profit per employee can rise simply through capital substitution, and requiring flat or falling gross plant isolates the intangible source from the mechanization source.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( growth( ratio( sub( sale, cogs ), emp ), 1 ) ), rank( neg( growth( ppegt, 1 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Irreversible Capacity Under Demand Uncertainty
input_signals.hypothesis: Physical capacity is irreversible while research spending can be throttled year to year, so firms facing volatile demand that nevertheless commit their investment budget to hard assets are exercising real options badly and earn lower subsequent returns.
input_signals.reasoning: The critic is right that the acquisition family is saturated — four different gates produced nearly identical alphas with flat slopes, which is evidence the aqc leg alone drives it — so this slot moves to an untested channel: the irreversibility-versus-flexibility distinction between tangible and intangible investment, which is the deepest economic difference between the two themes and one the archive has never exploited. The interaction is indispensable, since a hard-asset investment mix is perfectly sensible under stable demand and only becomes a real-options error when demand volatility is high.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( vol( growth( sale, 1 ), 5 ) ), rank( ratio( capx, add( capx, coalesce( xrd, 0 ) ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Hard Capital Stock Under Demand Uncertainty
input_signals.hypothesis: What matters under volatile demand is not only this year's allocation decision but the accumulated stock of sunk physical capital relative to flexible knowledge capital, because a firm already locked into plant cannot contract when demand disappoints.
input_signals.reasoning: Irreversible Capacity Under Demand Uncertainty is now the archive's best joint result (fmb -2.62, alpha -5.2%, t -3.74), and the first question for consolidation is whether the effect is a flow decision or a state of commitment; this replaces the one-year investment mix with the corresponding capital-stock composition while holding the uncertainty leg fixed. A stock formulation is also mechanically more stable than a single-year capex ratio, so it should raise coverage-quality and the cross-sectional slope if the commitment interpretation is right.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( vol( growth( sale, 1 ), 5 ) ), rank( ratio( ppent, add( ppent, ts_sum( coalesce( xrd, 0 ), 5 ) ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Externally Financed Hard Investment Mix
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ADD(sstk, DELTA(dltt, 1)), at)), RANK(RATIO(capx, ADD(capx, COALESCE(xrd, 0)))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Raising outside capital is most damaging when the proceeds are committed to replicable physical capacity rather than to knowledge creation, because investors fund a sunk expansion whose competitive advantage any rival can duplicate.
input_signals.reasoning: The archive's oldest joint winner paired external financing with the absence of R&D relative to sales, but the uncertainty result shows the hard-versus-soft budget share is a sharper and better-scaled expression of the same underlying distinction, with no zero-mass problem in the denominator; substituting it tests whether the financing penalty is about lacking knowledge or about where the money goes. This isolates a single well-defined design choice on a mechanism already validated on both metrics.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( add( sstk, delta( dltt, 1 ) ), at ) ), rank( ratio( capx, add( capx, coalesce( xrd, 0 ) ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Research Instability Normalized By Scale
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(VOL(RATIO(xrd, sale), 5), MA(RATIO(xrd, sale), 3))), RANK(RATIO(ppent, at)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Genuine instability in a research program is the variability of research intensity relative to its own average level, and an erratic innovation effort inside a capital-heavy firm signals an allocation process with neither strategic direction nor flexibility.
input_signals.reasoning: Unstable Research Program In A Capital-Heavy Firm came out significantly wrong-signed (fmb +2.24, alpha +2.1%), and the diagnosis is clean: raw VOL of R&D intensity scales with its level, so the leg was proxying for the R&D-intensity premium rather than for instability. Dividing by the three-year mean converts it into a coefficient of variation that is orthogonal to intensity by construction, which turns a failed signal into a real test of whether inconsistency, as opposed to magnitude, of knowledge investment is punished.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( vol( ratio( xrd, sale ), 5 ), ma( ratio( xrd, sale ), 3 ) ) ), rank( ratio( ppent, at ) ) )

input_signals.name: Capex Ramp Funded By Research Cuts
input_signals.hypothesis: When a firm raises capital spending in the same year it cuts research dollars, it is financing bricks by sacrificing knowledge, and the resulting shift toward replicable assets predicts low returns regardless of the level of either budget.
input_signals.reasoning: Rather than averaging two archived gates, this measures the substitution event itself in dollars, normalized by a smoothed revenue base, so a firm that raises both budgets or cuts both scores near zero and only genuine reallocation registers. It is distinct from the archived acceleration difference, which compared second differences of asset-scaled ratios and was dominated by capex noise, and from all the mix shares, which are level constructs that cannot see the direction of the swap.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: ratio( sub( delta( capx, 1 ), delta( coalesce( xrd, 0 ), 1 ) ), ma( sale, 3 ) )

input_signals.name: Inventory Efficiency From Rising Research
input_signals.hypothesis: Process and supply-chain knowledge shows up first as faster inventory turns, so a firm that is simultaneously raising research intensity and accelerating inventory turnover is converting intangible investment into operational efficiency the market has not priced.
input_signals.reasoning: The inventory channel has only ever been tested on the short side of this archive, as unwanted stock accumulation, and this uses it as the observable output of process innovation instead, which is a genuinely different economic reading of the same variable. Neither leg is spanned by the FF5 factors — inventory turnover growth is not asset growth and research-intensity change is not profitability — which addresses the concern that margin-improvement plus low-capex sorts merely restate CMA and RMW.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( growth( ratio( cogs, invt ), 1 ) ), rank( delta( ratio( coalesce( xrd, 0 ), sale ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Asset-Light Profit Scaling In Skill-Deep Firms
input_signals.hypothesis: Gross profit growing faster than physical plant is most informative at firms with deep human capital, measured as research dollars invested per employee, because there the scaling is powered by knowledge embodied in people rather than by capacity utilization.
input_signals.reasoning: The critic correctly noted that putting employment in the denominator of both legs makes the interaction load on headcount reduction, so employment now appears only in the conditioning leg while the active leg is the archive's validated asset-light gross-profit scaling measure. This isolates one clean question: whether human-capital depth is a better conditioning variable than research intensity scaled by sales on the archive's strongest long-side mechanism, with no mechanical layoff channel connecting the two legs.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( sub( growth( sub( sale, cogs ), 1 ), growth( ppegt, 1 ) ) ), rank( ratio( ts_sum( coalesce( xrd, 0 ), 3 ), emp ) ) )

input_signals.name: Reallocation Deflated By Knowledge-Inclusive Capital
input_signals.hypothesis: The economically meaningful size of a hard-for-soft reallocation is measured against the firm's existing capital base — plant plus accumulated knowledge — rather than against revenue, because it is the capital stock the reallocation is reshaping.
input_signals.reasoning: The champion signal deflates by smoothed sales, which mixes the reallocation with the firm's margin structure and asset turnover, so this isolates the deflator as a single design choice using a strictly positive, slow-moving denominator that directly represents the two capital types being traded off. It also connects the champion to the archive's other high-slope construction, the knowledge-inclusive capital deflator, which produced fmb -5.0 in a different application.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: ratio( sub( delta( capx, 1 ), delta( coalesce( xrd, 0 ), 1 ) ), add( ppent, ts_sum( coalesce( xrd, 0 ), 3 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Total Irreversible Commitment Swap
input_signals.hypothesis: Acquisitions and capital expenditure are both irreversible commitments, so the relevant reallocation is the change in total sunk spending net of the change in flexible research spending, and firms swapping into either hard channel while cutting knowledge investment underperform.
input_signals.reasoning: This brings the acquisition channel — which produced the archive's largest alphas but never a cross-sectional slope — into the one construct that does have a slope, not as another gate but as a component of a single budget aggregate, which is the first specification in which deal spending enters additively rather than as a zero-inflated conditioning rank. If the aggregate outperforms the capex-only champion, the irreversibility interpretation is confirmed and acquisitions are shown to matter through commitment rather than through a separate acquirer effect.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: ratio( sub( add( delta( capx, 1 ), delta( coalesce( aqc, 0 ), 1 ) ), delta( coalesce( xrd, 0 ), 1 ) ), ma( sale, 3 ) )

input_signals.name: Hard-Tilted Budget Relative To Own History
input_signals.hypothesis: What identifies a strategic tilt toward bricks is not this year's change but whether the firm's hard-minus-soft spending gap now sits at the top of its own five-year range, a state measure that is immune to industry spending norms and to one-off capital projects.
input_signals.reasoning: This is not a differencing-window tweak of the champion but a different object entirely: a within-firm position measure of the spending gap in levels rather than a difference of flows, which avoids the critic's point that a three-year difference of an annual flow mixes level drift with reallocation. Because each firm is benchmarked against itself, the sort carries no cross-sectional capital-intensity tilt, so a surviving alpha would show the reallocation effect is a firm-level regime change rather than a comparison between capital-heavy and knowledge-heavy businesses.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: ts_rank( ratio( sub( capx, coalesce( xrd, 0 ) ), ma( sale, 3 ) ), 5 )

input_signals.name: Funded Research Tilt With Profit Delivery
input_signals.hypothesis: Shifting the budget from capacity toward research is a bullish signal only when the firm's gross profit is simultaneously growing, since the same shift at a shrinking firm is capital rationing under distress rather than a deliberate investment in knowledge.
input_signals.reasoning: Rather than blending two correlated scaling measures under an unchanged gate, this addresses a specific unresolved question about the archive's champion: its long tail pools deliberate soft-tilting firms with distressed firms that simply cannot fund capex, and requiring contemporaneous gross-profit growth separates them. It is the first construct to use the reallocation measure as the active long-side leg, and it makes a falsifiable prediction — that the champion's long side is stronger once distress cases are screened out.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( neg( ratio( sub( delta( capx, 1 ), delta( coalesce( xrd, 0 ), 1 ) ), ma( sale, 3 ) ) ) ), rank( growth( sub( sale, cogs ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Capital Composition Drifting Toward Plant
input_signals.hypothesis: The consequence of repeated hard-for-soft reallocation is a capital base whose knowledge share is shrinking year after year, and this slow drift of composition toward replicable physical assets predicts low returns.
input_signals.reasoning: This abandons the exhausted three-year margin gate, which the critic correctly notes has delivered nearly identical alphas with flat slopes across four different investment legs and is most likely restating gross profitability, and instead asks whether the champion's flow effect shows up in the stock of capital it produces. The measure is a bounded share change with a strictly positive denominator, so it is far less tail-sensitive than the flow difference, and comparing the two tells us whether the market misprices the reallocation event or the accumulated composition it creates.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: neg( delta( ratio( ts_sum( coalesce( xrd, 0 ), 3 ), add( ppent, ts_sum( coalesce( xrd, 0 ), 3 ) ) ), 1 ) )

input_signals.name: Irreversible Commitment Gap At Own-History Extreme
input_signals.hypothesis: A firm is most exposed when its total sunk commitment — capital expenditure plus acquisition spending, net of flexible research spending — sits at the top of its own five-year range, because that is the point at which the firm has locked in the most irreversible capital it has ever carried relative to its revenue base.
input_signals.reasoning: Gen 7 produced two independent improvements on the champion reallocation idea, the own-history state formulation (fmb -5.71, alpha -4.8%, Sharpe -0.82) and the inclusion of acquisitions in the hard budget (fmb -4.81), and this is the one specification that tests whether they are complementary rather than substitutes. Because TS_RANK benchmarks each firm against itself, the lumpiness of acquisition spending that threatened the flow version is absorbed into the firm's own history rather than creating cross-sectional tail outliers.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: ts_rank( ratio( sub( add( capx, coalesce( aqc, 0 ) ), coalesce( xrd, 0 ) ), ma( sale, 3 ) ), 5 )

input_signals.name: Soft Tilt State With Profit Growth
input_signals.hypothesis: A firm whose spending gap has moved to the knowledge-tilted end of its own five-year history while its gross profit is still growing is deliberately funding innovation out of a healthy business, not rationing capital under distress.
input_signals.reasoning: Funded Research Tilt With Profit Delivery was the strongest long-side result ever recorded here (fmb 5.15, alpha +4.9%, t 4.99), and the parallel short-side evidence says the own-history state dominates the one-year flow difference, so substituting the state for the flow in the long-side construct is the natural consolidation and it holds the profit-delivery screen fixed for a clean comparison. Both legs remain non-negative ranks, so the product stays monotone and the distress cases that would otherwise pollute the knowledge-tilted tail are screened out by the profit requirement.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( neg( ts_rank( ratio( sub( capx, coalesce( xrd, 0 ) ), ma( sale, 3 ) ), 5 ) ) ), rank( growth( sub( sale, cogs ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Broad Intangible Budget Including Advertising
input_signals.hypothesis: Brand building is intangible investment of the same economic kind as research — expensed, flexible, and value-relevant — so the hard-versus-soft spending gap should be measured against total soft investment rather than research alone.
input_signals.reasoning: Advertising has never been usefully tested in this archive because cross-sectional constructions turned it into a consumer-industry reporting indicator, but inside a within-firm TS_RANK the comparison is always the same firm against itself, which is the one setting where the reporting-population problem does not bite. If the broad-soft version matches or beats the research-only champion, the mechanism is about flexibility versus irreversibility of investment generally rather than about research specifically.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: ts_rank( ratio( sub( capx, add( coalesce( xrd, 0 ), coalesce( xad, 0 ) ) ), ma( sale, 3 ) ), 5 )

input_signals.name: Hard Tilt Both Absolutely And Relative To Own History
input_signals.expression: SUMRANK(RATIO(SUB(capx, COALESCE(xrd, 0)), MA(sale, 3)), TS_RANK(RATIO(SUB(capx, COALESCE(xrd, 0)), MA(sale, 3)), 5))
input_signals.hypothesis: The most exposed firms are those whose spending gap is hard-tilted both against their industry-wide peer distribution and against their own five-year history, since a high absolute commitment that is also unusual for the firm identifies a fresh, aggressive shift rather than a stable business model.
input_signals.reasoning: The critic's own argument establishes that TS_RANK strips out all cross-firm heterogeneity, which means the champion discards the level information entirely and cannot distinguish a chronically capital-intensive firm at its own peak from a knowledge-heavy firm making the same relative move; adding the cross-sectional rank restores that orthogonal dimension rather than adjusting a deflator that leaves the within-firm ordering nearly unchanged. This is the only way to test whether the two rankings carry complementary information, and SUMRANK keeps both components bounded so neither dominates through outliers.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: sumrank( ratio( sub( capx, coalesce( xrd, 0 ) ), ma( sale, 3 ) ), ts_rank( ratio( sub( capx, coalesce( xrd, 0 ) ), ma( sale, 3 ) ), 5 ) )

input_signals.name: Externally Funded Hard Tilt State
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(TS_RANK(RATIO(SUB(capx, COALESCE(xrd, 0)), MA(sale, 3)), 5)), RANK(RATIO(ADD(sstk, DELTA(dltt, 1)), at)))
input_signals.hypothesis: A shift to the firm's most hard-tilted spending posture is far more damaging when it is financed by newly raised outside capital, because internally funded capacity building is disciplined by cash generation while externally funded building is not.
input_signals.reasoning: The critic is right that conditioning the hard-tilt state on gross-profit decline is algebraically almost the mirror of conditioning the soft-tilt state on gross-profit growth, so this replaces the profit dimension with an economically independent one — the funding source — which the archive has separately validated (external financing paired with the hard investment mix produced fmb -2.76, alpha -3.2%, Sharpe -0.26). The question it answers is new and sharp: whether the reallocation penalty is an overinvestment story about where money is spent or a financing story about where the money came from.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ts_rank( ratio( sub( capx, coalesce( xrd, 0 ) ), ma( sale, 3 ) ), 5 ) ), rank( ratio( add( sstk, delta( dltt, 1 ) ), at ) ) )

input_signals.name: Plant Stock At Own-History Peak Against Knowledge-Inclusive Scale
input_signals.hypothesis: When a firm's physical capital base reaches its own five-year high relative to the combined scale of its revenue and its accumulated knowledge capital, the accumulated overbuild is at its most extreme and subsequent returns are low.
input_signals.reasoning: The degeneracy the critic identified is removed because the denominator now contains a smoothed revenue term, so the ratio varies through time for firms that report no research and they are ranked on their own genuine capital-intensity history instead of piling at a constant extreme. The construct still tests the stock analogue of the champion — accumulated physical commitment measured against a knowledge-inclusive scale — while retaining the low-turnover, slow-moving portfolio composition that makes it a useful contrast with the flow-based signals.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: ts_rank( ratio( ppent, add( ts_sum( coalesce( xrd, 0 ), 5 ), ma( sale, 3 ) ) ), 5 )

input_signals.name: Hard Tilt Against Gross Profit Capacity
input_signals.hypothesis: The burden of a hard-tilted budget should be judged against the profit stream that must fund and service it, not against revenue, because a given capacity commitment is far heavier for a thin-margin firm than for a firm earning large rents on each sales dollar.
input_signals.reasoning: The critic correctly rejected a capital-stock deflator because a near-constant denominator leaves the within-firm ordering unchanged, but smoothed gross profit varies substantially through time and encodes margin compression, so this deflator genuinely alters which years rank as extreme for a given firm. It also folds the pricing-power information that produced repeated short-side alphas into the champion construct without adding a separate margin gate, which the archive has shown to contribute alpha but no slope.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: ts_rank( ratio( sub( capx, coalesce( xrd, 0 ) ), ma( sub( sale, cogs ), 3 ) ), 5 )

input_signals.name: Hard Tilt State Under Demand Uncertainty
input_signals.hypothesis: Reaching one's most hard-tilted spending posture is most damaging when demand is volatile, because irreversible capital committed into an unstable revenue stream cannot be unwound when the trough arrives.
input_signals.reasoning: Demand uncertainty paired with the hard-soft investment mix produced the largest short-side alpha before the reallocation family appeared (-5.2%, t -3.74) and remains the only conditioning variable with a real-options rationale, whereas the external-financing gate tested in gen 8 preserved the slope but cut the alpha to -1.9%, indicating financing is not where the mispricing lives. Substituting the far stronger own-history state for the mix leg is the natural final test of whether uncertainty amplifies the champion mechanism.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ts_rank( ratio( sub( capx, coalesce( xrd, 0 ) ), ma( sale, 3 ) ), 5 ) ), rank( vol( growth( sale, 1 ), 5 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Soft Tilt State With Rising Labor Productivity
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(NEG(TS_RANK(RATIO(SUB(capx, COALESCE(xrd, 0)), MA(sale, 3)), 5))), RANK(GROWTH(RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), emp), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: A knowledge-tilted budget is validated not by aggregate profit growth, which can come from scale or acquisitions, but by rising gross profit per employee, which shows the intangible investment is raising the productivity of the people who carry it.
input_signals.reasoning: The archive's long-side evidence rests on two different confirmations of intangible payoff — aggregate gross-profit growth and labor-productivity growth, the latter producing alpha of +4.5% with t 4.32 — and only the first has been paired with the reallocation state, leaving open whether the long-side result is a plain growth effect or a genuine productivity effect. Because per-employee profit growth is scale-free, this specification is far less exposed to the size and growth tilts that could be inflating the aggregate-profit version.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( neg( ts_rank( ratio( sub( capx, coalesce( xrd, 0 ) ), ma( sale, 3 ) ), 5 ) ) ), rank( growth( ratio( sub( sale, cogs ), emp ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Jump Into A Hard-Tilted Regime
input_signals.hypothesis: What the market misprices is the transition itself — a firm moving from the knowledge-tilted part of its own history to the capacity-tilted part within a single year — rather than the standing level of the tilt.
input_signals.reasoning: The archive has established that both the flow event and the state level are priced, but not whether the state's predictive content comes from its position or from the recent movement in that position, and differencing the within-firm rank isolates the regime change while automatically neutralizing each firm's structural capital intensity. It is a distinct object from the flow reallocation ratio, which is denominated in dollars and dominated by large projects, whereas this is a bounded movement in percentile space that treats a small but decisive shift in a stable firm as informative.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: delta( ts_rank( ratio( sub( capx, coalesce( xrd, 0 ) ), ma( sale, 3 ) ), 5 ), 1 )

input_signals.name: Inventory-Inclusive Commitment Tilt State
input_signals.hypothesis: Stock built for future sale is a commitment of the same economic kind as plant — cash sunk into physical goods that can only be recovered by selling them, often at a discount — so the relevant hard budget is capital expenditure plus inventory accumulation measured against flexible research spending.
input_signals.reasoning: This is a composition test of the hard side of the budget rather than a blend of two archived signals, and it is the direct analogue of the acquisition-inclusive test that proved informative in gen 8: there deal spending was folded in additively and slightly weakened the result, telling us the mechanism is not about acquirers, and here the same question is asked of working-capital commitment, which the archive has only ever tested as a standalone leg with a margin gate. Within-firm ranking keeps the lumpy inventory change benchmarked against the firm's own history rather than against structurally inventory-heavy peers.
